title: Why weren't you Zusya?
hook: Reb Zusya feared being asked not why he wasn't Moses, but why he wasn't Zusya

segments.voice: Yesterday each generation lost the fire, the prayer and the place, but kept the story. Your line was the story is enough. Did you tell one? Day two hundred ninety-eight.

Scroll for thirty seconds and you'll find someone doing your life better. A better parent, a better runner, a better cook, a kinder friend, with better lighting. It's easy to measure yourself against all of them and come up short every time. Now picture an old Hasidic rebbe, much loved, lying on his deathbed. His students gather around him, and they're surprised to see that he's afraid. He's crying. They ask him why. And his answer has been passed from person to person ever since.
screen: `SOMEONE DOING YOUR LIFE BETTER.` → `AN OLD REBBE, AFRAID.` → `WHY ARE YOU CRYING?`

segments.voice: The rebbe is Zusya of Hanipol, an early Hasidic teacher. He was a student of the Maggid of Mezritch, the Baal Shem Tov's successor, and he was known as a humble, joyful, often penniless man, so gentle that people told stories about his kindness. As the story goes, his students tried to comfort him. Rebbe, you've been as faithful as Moses, as kind as Abraham. Surely you have nothing to fear. And Zusya answered, roughly: when I get to the world to come, they won't ask me, Zusya, why weren't you Moses? They won't ask, why weren't you Abraham? They'll ask me: Zusya, why weren't you Zusya? And what will I say? That's the whole story. It turns the usual fear upside down. The worry isn't failing to be someone greater. It's failing to be yourself. Not a copy of Moses. The whole of Zusya, with his own gifts and his own work. In Jewish tradition every person is created in the image of God, and no two people are alike. Zusya takes that seriously. In the story, there's a Zusya-shaped job in the world, and only Zusya can do it. The story is mostly known through modern collections of Hasidic tales, and the exact words differ from teller to teller. But the question has lasted, because it travels so easily.
screen: `THE REBBE ON HIS DEATHBED.` · `NOT: WHY WEREN'T YOU MOSES?` · `WHY WEREN'T YOU ZUSYA?` · `ONLY YOU CAN BE YOU.` · then, large: `BE ZUSYA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: meet your own Zusya. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you often compare yourself to. Let them go for now. Instead ask: what's something I do that's really mine? A kind of humor, a way of listening, a thing I notice that others miss, a skill my hands have. Name one. Now picture doing a little more of that today. Not to impress anyone. Just to be a little more you. The bell holds the time.
Zusya, the Hasidic rebbe who on his deathbed feared not being asked why he wasn't Moses, but why he wasn't fully himself.
Your line: be zusya. Today, stop comparing for one hour, and do one thing that's truly yours. Day two hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Reb Zusya's question is a widely quoted Hasidic saying, used by rabbis and teachers to encourage people to become fully themselves rather than copies of others.

sources.ref: Hasidic tale attributed to Zusya of Hanipol

notes: Paraphrased; the best-known English version is in Martin Buber's Tales of the Hasidim (copyrighted), so nothing is quoted. Zusya's words are rendered 'roughly'.
Zusya of Hanipol (Annopol), died 1800; brother of Elimelech of Lizhensk; student of the Maggid of Mezritch.
'No two people are alike' echoes Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 (God stamps all people with one seal, yet none is like another); cited as paraphrase.
Zusya's name is Yiddish; original set to null.
